Text: $TSM $SPCX $PLTR $NVDA Monday, October 19, 1987—known as Black Monday—was the worst single-day percentage decline in the history of the Dow Jones Industrial Average. The Dow fell 22.61%, losing 508 points in one trading session. And there is a striking calendar coincidence: October 19, 2026, is also a Monday, exactly 39 years later. Author: TheQuietBull
Text: Samsung Electronics will use TSMC's 3nm process to make base dies for Nvidia's next generation custom HBM chips. The move marks the first time Samsung has worked with TSMC at the HBM manufacturing stage and it comes after Nvidia ($NVDA) asked Samsung ($SSNLF), SK Hynix ($SKHY) and Micron ($MU) to standardize NVHBM base dies on TSMC ($TSM) 3nm and core dies on 1c DRAM. Nvidia is forcing the whole HBM supply chain to look the same so it does not have to validate three different designs. For Samsung this is a concession after years of pushing its own 4nm turnkey HBM4 and HBM4E, and it opens the door for Samsung foundry to try to win back NVHBM volume later if TSMC capacity tightens. Watch $NVDA and $TSM into Monday open, $SSNLF and $SKHY in Seoul Monday, and $MU for HBM margin read. If TSMC 3nm capacity talk hits, Samsung foundry option becomes the swing and HBM pricing power shifts back to Nvidia. Not financial advice.

Author: SilverTrader47
Text: @Palmetto_Trader Before Pat Gelsinger became $INTC CEO in 2021, Intel had already fallen significantly behind $TSM in semiconductor manufacturing technology. Intel remained heavily dependent on its 14nm process for years, struggled with repeated delays in bringing its 10nm process into production, and subsequently encountered serious yield problems with its 7nm process. Meanwhile, TSMC had already moved to 7nm production in 2018 and 5nm in 2020. Intel's manufacturing setbacks also contributed to Apple's decision to transition away from Intel processors in its Mac computers, announcing the switch to Apple-designed M-series chips in June 2020, manufactured by TSMC. This multi-year decline in manufacturing leadership weakened Intel's competitiveness and encouraged companies like AMD, Apple, and NVIDIA to rely increasingly on TSMC for advanced chip manufacturing.

Text: $NVDA CEO Clue? Why CUDA Creator Ian Buck Taking the SC26 Stage Matters: Back in 2000 at Stanford, grad student Ian Buck wanted to play fast-paced shooters (Quake III & Doom) on a giant 8K wall without buying a multimillion-dollar supercomputer. Text: $AVGO $NVDA $TSM $AMD $DELL I’m bullish on AI, but that doesn’t mean I’m ignoring the risks. What would actually make me bearish? • Hyperscalers cutting CapEx and cancelling orders. • TSMC reporting declining capacity utilization. • Broadcom and NVIDIA lowering AI revenue guidance. • Memory prices falling due to excess inventory. • Deteriorating margins and free cash flow. • AI infrastructure providers struggling to service their debt. Instead, we’re seeing record revenues, record backlogs, rising prices, expanding margins and demand exceeding production capacity. There are legitimate concerns about AI monetization, excessive spending and financing sustainability. But those risks need to be evaluated individually, not indiscriminately applied to every company in the AI ecosystem. Right now, I see a crisis of confidence in AI, not a crisis in the AI industry itself.

Here’s how I classify the risks facing the AI and semiconductor industry: Risk | Short-term impact | Long-term impact • Higher interest rates: High / Low–Moderate • Mild recession: Moderate / Potentially positive for AI adoption • Severe recession: High / Moderate–High • Margin normalization: Moderate / Low–Moderate • Financing difficulties: High for smaller players / Moderate • CapEx deceleration: High / Depends on duration • China invading Taiwan: Extreme / Potentially catastrophic A recession could actually accelerate AI adoption as companies seek to reduce costs, automate processes and improve productivity, although infrastructure spending could temporarily slow. AI is both a growth technology and a cost-reduction technology. Economic cycles are manageable. A major disruption of Taiwan’s semiconductor manufacturing capacity is an entirely different story.
